The ship wrecked off Uluburun in Turkey carried 354 oxhide ingots, about ten tonnes of copper, with roughly a tonne of tin and nine Cypriot storage jars packed with pottery, oil or pomegranates. The lead isotopes of the copper point back to the Solea mines. Excavated by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology from 1984 to 1994.

en: In situ, Apliki mine

A sanctuary in the hills south of Myrtou, used from about 1650 BCE to the end of the Bronze Age and excavated in 1949 and 1950 by Joan du Plat Taylor and Veronica Seton-Williams for the Department of Antiquities. Its courtyard holds a stepped altar of dressed stone crowned with carved horns, the Cretan sign of sanctity known as horns of consecration, rebuilt on the spot by the excavators. The wells that give the place its name, pigadhes, supplied the rites. Bones of sheep, goat and deer, hearths and a mass of drinking vessels point to sacrifice and feasting in the open rather than to a temple with a resident priesthood.
The horned altar

A stepped block-built altar in the west court, re-erected by the excavators with a pair of stone horns on top. It is the largest and best preserved of its kind on Cyprus and the plainest borrowing of Minoan religious symbolism on the island; what stands today is a reconstruction, and its exact original height is not certain.

en: The Late Bronze Age town of the lower Kouris valley, on a low hill by Episkopi a short way inland from the sea, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania Museum from 1934 under Bertram Hill, George McFadden and John Franklin Daniel. Six hectares of planned housing with streets and wells, an outer town and a fortified inner town on the hill, and the dead buried among the living in single-chamber tombs. Its seals and writing tools give the best stratified sequence for Cypriot administration and for the island's earliest writing; it was never sacked, but drifted into abandonment by the later twelfth century BCE, and the population later gathered on the cliff at Kourion above.
Bamboula hill and its circuit wall

A fortification wall thrown round the inner town in the thirteenth century BCE, with the open outer town spreading beyond it. The hill is the visible remnant of a place that once functioned as the harbour arm of an inland polity, probably centred at Alassa.

Tripartite houses
Late Cypriot II
Rectangular dwellings of five or six rooms on stone footings with mudbrick above, each a distinct household unit on a laid-out street grid rather than an organic huddle.

Seals used both as administrative devices and as personal ornaments, found with the metal styli used to cut Cypro-Minoan signs into clay. Because they come from a stratified settlement rather than from looted tombs, they underpin the dating of Cypriot seals and of the script.

en: A cemetery of some seven square kilometres west of the city, where nine great built chamber tombs of the late eighth to early sixth centuries BCE were approached by long ramps. Horses in harness were killed at the ramp mouth and left where they fell, sometimes still yoked to a chariot or a hearse, and the burials were furnished with ivory furniture, bronze cauldrons, jars of oil and honey and imported Levantine and Greek pottery. Vassos Karageorghis and Porphyrios Dikaios began systematic excavation in 1957; every chamber had already been robbed, so almost everything known comes from the ramps and the forecourts. The resemblance to the funeral of Patroklos in the Iliad has been argued over ever since, some reading it as living Homeric practice and others as eighth-century kings deliberately staging an ancestral past.

en: In situ; clay figures in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

The main cemetery of Palaepaphos at the moment the Bronze Age ended and the Iron Age began, about a kilometre south-east of the town. Bulldozing for farmland exposed the tombs, and more than fifty chamber graves were dug in the winter and spring of 1979 under Vassos Karageorghis, with further rescue work down to 2011. The dead were laid in chambers reached by long sloping passages, with bronze bowls, gold and faience jewellery, iron weapons and the roasting spits that mark a meat-eating warrior elite. Because one of those spits carries a Greek name in the local syllabary, Skales is the single site most often cited for the arrival of Greek speakers on Cyprus.
Tomb 49

A chamber tomb holding three bronze roasting spits, one of them inscribed in the syllabary with the genitive of a Greek personal name, Opheltas. The tomb is the find context for the earliest Greek text from the island, and the reading of the last sign is still discussed.
In situ (backfilled); contents in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia
Bimetallic knives
11th–10th century BCE

Knives with iron blades riveted into bronze or ivory handles, among the earliest worked iron on Cyprus. They show local smiths mastering the new metal while the old one was still the prestige material.
Proto-White Painted pottery
The first pottery of the Iron Age, decorated with Aegean-derived motifs but made in Cypriot shapes, in quantity here for the first time. Skales gave the type its stratigraphic anchor.

Gold spiral earrings, embossed sheet-gold mouthpieces and diadems, and faience and glass beads of Egyptian and Levantine type. They show that Paphos was still trading east while the Aegean palaces were in ruins.

en: Cremation burials
11th–9th century BCE

A minority of the dead were burned and their bones gathered into jars, a practice new to Cyprus at this date. Recent osteological work on the cremated bone is being used to test whether the rite marks incomers or a new fashion among locals.
Studied material with the Department of Antiquities, Cyprus
Tomb 277
11th century BCE

One of the later-excavated graves, unusually well furnished with bronze vessels and weapons and published in 2021. Its contents strengthened the case that a small hereditary elite at Paphos survived the Bronze Age collapse intact.

The cemetery on the saddle below the Kourion bluff, and for a long time the only real evidence for the early history of the kingdom, since the Iron Age town itself has never been found. The University of Pennsylvania Museum expedition dug here in the 1930s, and its tombs run from the eleventh century BCE to Classical times, with the Cypro-Geometric graves the richest. Their bronze vessels and Aegean-style pottery were once read as the graves of Argive founders arriving after the Trojan War; the current reading is more cautious, and speaks of local elites who chose Aegean things.
The Kourion sceptre

A short gold staff whose head is a globe of cloisonné enamel surmounted by two falcons, about 16 cm long. The enamelling has no Aegean parallel and looks Egyptian in technique, and it is one of the earliest true enamels anywhere; it is usually called royal, though the tomb was disturbed and the claim cannot be proved.

en: Tomb 40
First half of the 11th century BCE

A shaft grave holding a cremation in a bronze vessel, two bronze rod tripod stands, the remains of a shield and the gold sceptre. Once described as the tomb of the Achaean founder of Kourion, it is now more often read as the grave of a Cypriot or Phoenician notable.

Bronze rod tripod stands
12th–11th century BCE

Openwork stands of cast bronze rods made to carry a bowl, a Cypriot speciality of the very end of the Bronze Age. Examples travelled to Crete and the Greek mainland, and they are the clearest sign that Cypriot smiths were still exporting skill after the palaces fell.

en: A small country sanctuary on the northern approaches to the Troodos, near the copper ground of Mitsero, excavated by the Department of Antiquities under Vassos Karageorghis in the early 1970s and published with a second shrine in 1977. It matters because the deity worshipped in it was not Greek: the cult statuary is of the Phoenician Baal Hamman, the bearded god enthroned between rams, in a village well inland from Phoenician Kition. Meniko is the standard evidence that Phoenician religion reached the Cypriot countryside and not only the coastal city, probably along the road to the mines.
Limestone statue of an enthroned bearded god
Later 6th century BCE

A seated male figure with a long squared beard on a throne whose arms end in rams' heads, the standard image of Baal Hamman. No inscription names him, so the identification rests on the iconography, which is why some prefer the neutral 'enthroned god'.

en: In situ, Meniko (unroofed and largely reburied)
Terracotta votives

Mould-made and handmade clay figures, including horse-and-rider groups and bulls, left by ordinary visitors. They are the same repertoire found at Greek-dedicated shrines on the island, which is the point: the offerings were Cypriot even when the god was not.

A cave shrine to a Nymph on a conical hill south-east of Nicosia, dug in 1939 and again between 1949 and 1955 and published by Terence Mitford in 1980. It produced some 310 inscribed pots and terracottas, of which 269 were dedicated by one man: Onesagoras son of Philounios, a barber who gave himself the title dekatephoros, tithe-bringer. The dedications are dated between 225 and 218 BCE and many are written out twice, once in the Cypriot syllabary and once in the Greek alphabet, which pushed the survival of the old script down to the end of the third century BCE. It is the best evidence anywhere for how an ordinary Cypriot under the Ptolemies actually spoke to a god.
The inscribed vessels of Onesagoras

About 310 pots, of which 269 were dedicated by Onesagoras, inscribed before and after firing with dates, quantities and addresses to the Nymph. They read like a working ledger crossed with prayer, and they carry precise regnal dates, which is why the group anchors so much Cypriot chronology.

en: A rural sanctuary of Aphrodite in the eastern Mesaoria, known from inscriptions that call the goddess Golgia, the Aphrodite of Golgoi, so the shrine belonged to a cult network rather than standing alone. Its votive deposit was unusual for containing mostly female statues, which makes it the best single source for how Cypriot sculptors handled women, from stiff Archaic figures in heavy jewellery to softened Hellenistic types. The finds were dispersed in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the shrine has never been properly excavated or securely located on the ground.

The finds were divided between sponsors and are now spread across the British Museum, the Louvre, the Pierides Museum and the Cyprus Museum.

An unwalled town spread over the neck and southern slope of Cape Drepanon, busy in the Roman period and at its height under Justinian, when three basilicas and a bath house stood on the headland. Its position at the island's north-west corner made it a natural call for ships carrying Egyptian grain to Constantinople, and the sherd dumps show it shipped wine of its own as well. The Department of Antiquities dug the churches between 1952 and 1955; the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki from 1992 and the Greek Archaeological Expedition since 1999 have worked on the settlement itself, which turned what had looked like a pilgrimage complex into a proper town.

en: A flat-topped islet of about 2.6 hectares rising some 21 m out of the sea a short way off Cape Drepanon, its name meaning Holy Island. Sophocles Hadjisavvas began digging in 1982 when a hotel was proposed for it, and Joan Breton Connelly of New York University has directed the excavation since 1990. In the last decades of Ptolemaic rule, under Cleopatra VII, a striking amount of money went into turning the rock into a sanctuary of Apollo with its own kitchens, stores and lookout; it was abandoned after an earthquake around the turn of the era. Chalcolithic remains lie beneath the Hellenistic buildings and a Byzantine reservoir and animal shelters above them.
The 'Apollo' ostrakon

A potsherd inscribed with the god's name, and the only object that actually names the divinity of Holy Island. The identification of the sanctuary rests on this sherd and on amulets that match ones from Apollo shrines elsewhere on Cyprus.
Paphos District Archaeological Museum
Ptolemaic ostraka
The only Ptolemaic ostraka found on Cyprus, written in Greek and concerned with the running of the sanctuary and its stores. Ostraka of this kind are common in Egypt and almost unknown on the island.
Stone parapegma
A slab pierced with a row of holes for a peg to be shifted along through the days of the month, a working calendar of a kind rare anywhere in the Greek world.
Limestone amulets

Small pierced amulets shaped rather like miniature loom weights, cut with a mixture of old Cypriot and Ptolemaic Egyptian motifs. Twenty-five years of digging have produced a whole series, and they are the strongest argument for what kind of cult was practised here.
The circular platform
A paved circle in the middle of the island that Connelly reads as a dance floor used in rites of passage for boys. That is an interpretation and not a certainty, and other readings are possible.

en: In situ, Yeronisos
The southern service range

A complex of rooms for preparing, distributing and storing food, built along the island's southern edge in the final years of Ptolemaic rule; in one room the plaster of the ground floor is still on the wall.

en: Chalcolithic pestles and mortars
c. 3800 BCE

Stone tools from the island's first occupation, many found in the Hellenistic food-preparation area where they appear to have been picked up and put back to work three and a half thousand years later.

en: A church complex about 100 m long standing on its own in the western forest of the Akrotiri peninsula, surveyed from 2007 and excavated by Eleni Procopiou for the Department of Antiquities. Its main church is a three-aisled basilica 36 m wide and 29 m long crossed by a transverse aisle, a transept plan otherwise unknown on Cyprus and rare in the eastern Mediterranean. Pottery and inscriptions place its building in the first years of the reign of Heraclius, about 616 to 619, and its destruction shortly before the middle of the seventh century. Why so grand and so unusual a building was raised on an empty headland is still argued over.
